abstract:
The liver-brain axis has emerged as a critical pathway in depression pathogenesis, yet the molecular basis of this crosstalk remains largely unexplored. Chaihu-Shugan-San (CSS), a classic Traditional Chinese Medicine formula for "soothing the liver and relieving depression" has shown both hepatoprotective and antidepressant effects, but whether these actions are linked via the liver-brain axis and through what molecular mechanism remains unknown.
This study aimed to determine whether Chaihu-Shugan-San (CSS) exerts antidepressant effects via the liver-brain axis and to elucidate the mediating role of liver lipocalin 2 (LCN2) and its receptor SLC22A17 in regulating lateral habenula (LHb) function.
A chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) mouse model was established. CSS (2, 4, 8 g/kg) or fluoxetine (10 mg/kg) was orally administered. Depressive-like behaviors were assessed by sucrose preference, open field, and forced swim tests. Hepatic injury was evaluated by serum ALT/AST and H&E staining. Liver transcriptomics and LHb single-cell RNA sequencing were performed to identify key molecules, followed by qRT-PCR, Western blot, ELISA, and immunofluorescence for validation. The causal role of LCN2 was tested via liver-specific AAV-mediated overexpression.
CSS ameliorated CUMS-induced depressive-like behaviors and liver injury. Transcriptomics and PPI network analysis identified Lcn2 as a hub gene. CSS reversed CUMS-induced elevation of LCN2 in the liver, serum, and LHb, as well as the upregulation of its receptor SLC22A17 in the LHb. LHb single-cell sequencing revealed that CSS restored CUMS-induced changes in astrocyte subcluster ASC6, including downregulation of AQP4 and SLC38A1 and impaired intercellular communication. Consequently, CSS reduced the elevated expression of c-FOS and GluN2B and restored AQP4 and SLC38A1 in the LHb. Importantly, liver-specific Lcn2 overexpression recapitulated CUMS-like depressive phenotypes and LHb abnormalities, including elevated SLC22A17 and GluN2B, and largely abolished the antidepressant effects of CSS.
CSS ameliorates depressive-like behaviors in association with downregulation of hepatic LCN2 and its candidate receptor SLC22A17 in the LHb, restoring ASC6-mediated glutamate homeostasis, and suppressing GluN2B-related Glutamatergic Signaling. These findings are consistent with a model in which LHb function may be modulated via the liver-brain axis through hepatic LCN2 and its candidate receptor SLC22A17, although the direct source of LHb LCN2 remains to be determined, offering experimental support for the scientific basis of CSS in "soothing the liver and relieving depression."
